questions.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ for which ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=15$ are eigenvalues, and

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

are the respective eigenvectors. What are the values of $a,b,c$ given that

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ 2 & c\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}a & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & b \\ 2 & c\end{aligned}]}^{-1}?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=15,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=15.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

 

In conclusion, we get $a=3,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=1.$

questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -3 & 5\end{aligned}]$ 
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -3 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-(1)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +5+3 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable.

Now, we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 4 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-1-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-4\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-1I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗ \\ 2 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the second column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-(1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}10 & -12 \\ 8 & -10\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & ∗ \\ -1 & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ find the second column of the matrix $P.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -12 \\ 8 & -10\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 \\ 8 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 & 0 \\ 8 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}8 & -12 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -6 & -7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & -1 \\ b & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of  $\frac{b}{a}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

So, the  first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ Computing $A-(-4)I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -6 & -7\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ -6 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{2}{-1}=-2.$

$$

questions.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal:  

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=4\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=1$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 
The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 8 \\ -3 & 8\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ using its characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & 8 \\ -3 & 8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(8-\lambda )-(8)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -24 & =0 \\ (\lambda +4)(\lambda -6) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 8 \\ -3 & 8\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 8 \\ -3 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 8 & 0 \\ -3 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=4{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-6I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 8 \\ -3 & 8\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 8 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 
So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 8 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-12 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=E,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $E=[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm. 

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $E$ using its characteristic equation $det(E-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 9 \\ -6 & -8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(-8-\lambda )-9\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $E$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $E.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E-I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 \\ -6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 & 0 \\ -6 & -9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 \\ -6 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 & 0 \\ -6 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. On the other hand, from the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-2\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=4,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 5 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{4}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Its Eigenvalues
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the matrix $[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -5 & 4\end{aligned}]$ You're given that $\lambda_1=4$ and $\lambda_2=3$ are the eigenvalues of $A,$ and
$[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PDP^{-1} = A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are $\lambda_1={\color{blue}4}$ and $\lambda_2={\color{red}3},$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1={\color{blue}4},$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_2={\color{red}3}.$

Therefore, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable
canonical_examples.problem:
Determine if the matrix
$[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=3.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $A-3I\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D=P^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1= -{2}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

By setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-2}{1} = -2.$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given the matrix 
$[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D=P^{-1}AP.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm. 

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$$
\lambda_1=3, \quad\quad\lambda_2=-2.
$$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{8}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, $x_1$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_2=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$

- For $\lambda_2=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix corresponds to a homogeneous system of linear equations. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac{8}{5}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

Setting  $x_2=5,$ we get the eigenvector  $[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 5\end{aligned}]$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$
